title: Chapter 69: Fire at the Edge, Part 2 of 5: The Last Bread
html:
They took the stones out of the fire at sunset.
The men did it, with the long forked sticks, one stone at a time, lifting each one out of the red heart of the fire and swinging it, glowing dull red at the edges and smoking, onto a flat bed of gravel to cool. The heat came off them in waves. You could not stand near them. The air above them shook. When the women came with the felt, they wrapped each stone in three thick layers, fast, with their hands bound in wet rags, and tied the bundles with thongs, and the felt smoked and smelled of singed wool, and did not burn.
Ten bundles. One for each walker. Lined up on the gravel by the fire like a row of small gray loaves.
Lyra picked hers up. It was as heavy as a brick and hot all the way through, even through the three layers of felt, so hot she could hardly hold it. She held it against her chest anyway, and closed her eyes, and felt the heat go into her. She had been cold for so long. Since the fens. Since the dyke road. Since before that. She had forgotten what it was like to be warm right through.
"Don't get used to it," said Vespera, beside her. "It won't last."
The old woman was sitting on a mat by the fire with her own stone in her lap and her blue hands spread over it, palms down, like someone warming herself at a stove. She had her rope belt back on. All her needles in their places. She looked smaller than ever, wrapped in a borrowed Ashborn fur over her crushed dark coat.
"Nothing does," said Lyra.
Vespera looked up at her. The slit of her mouth went up at one corner.
"No," she said. "That's the first true thing anybody's said to me all day. Sit down."
Lyra sat down.
The camp ate together that night. All of it, round the big fire, the way it had on the night of the rite. Everybody. The ten who were going and the ones who were staying. There was bread, fresh, the soft kind, not the hard dried rounds for the Glass. Lyra had made some of it. Two of hers were burnt. Nobody said anything. There was broth with goat meat in it, and the black berries, and a pot of something hot and sweet made from honey and the dried apples and goat's milk, that the children were given first and fought over.
It was not a sad meal. Lyra had thought it would be. It was not. The Ashborn laughed. They told stories, in their round slow speech, and the ones who could talk the southern way told them to Lyra and Oren and Corin and Vespera too, leaning across with their bowls. Stories about Old Hask. About the winter he had walked into the goat pen in the dark thinking it was his tent and slept all night among the goats and woken up saying he had never been so warm. About the time he had beaten three young men at stones, blind, and then told them he had cheated, and would not say how. Everybody had a story about Hask. Everybody laughed. And the laughing was a kind of carrying too, Lyra thought. A way of passing him round the fire, so that nobody held too much.
Corin was sitting a little way along from her.
He was not laughing. But he was listening. She could see it in his face, the way it went quiet and open, listening. And every now and then, when a story ended and the laughter went round, she heard it. Very faint. Under the noise. The hum. Round and round, up a little and down a little, in the back of his throat.
He did not know he was doing it.
She did not tell him.
Oren was on her other side, eating bread with both hands as if he had not eaten for a week, which, after two hundred and one swings of a thorn stick, he possibly had not. The goat that loved him was lying against his back. He had stopped pushing it away.
"Tonight," he said, around a mouthful. Low. To her and to Corin. "Tonight they'll be on the moor. Past Haverstock. Cold. Coming up to the Lip tomorrow, if they come straight. That's what I make it." He chewed. "So tomorrow night, we go."
"Two fingers," said Corin.
Oren looked at him. Then he grinned, in his beard.
"Two fingers," he said.
Lyra knew what that meant. She had leaned over to Oren last night, by the fire, and whispered to him to show it that way, with his fingers, not with numbers, because she had seen Corin's face when the numbers went past him. And Oren had understood at once, and done it, and never said a word about it since. Now it was a thing between the two of them. And she found, to her surprise, that she was glad of that. Glad there was something between them that she did not have to carry.
She ate her bread. Her burnt one.
Across the fire, Kestrel was sitting with the five. Arran and Brin and Oda and Sef and Marrit. They were not laughing as much as the others. They were sitting close together, with their bowls, and talking low, and every now and then Marrit, the old one, would say something, and the others would listen very carefully. Lyra thought it was probably about the Glass. About the cairns. About which way.
And behind them, at the edge of the light, the children who had to stay were sitting in a row, wrapped in furs, with their spears across their knees. Pretending to be sentries. Pretending they did not mind. The girl who had thrown her spear down was at the end of the row, with her spear back in her hand, very straight, looking out into the dark toward the south.
Looking out for whatever was coming.
The fire crackled. The stones in their felt cooled on the gravel. The stars came out over the ridge, one by one, and then all at once.
And somebody, somewhere among the tents, picked up a drum.
The Dance
It was a small drum. A hoop of bent wood with a goat skin stretched over it, tight as a tambour, and painted with a gray hand in the middle. A young man held it under his arm and beat it with the flat of his fingers. Not loud. A soft, quick, rolling beat, like rain on a roof, like a heart running.
Then another drum joined it. Bigger, deeper, from the other side of the fire. Thump. Thump. Slow under the quick one, like a foot stamping.
And then the clapping.
It started with the old women. They clapped on the slow beat, not hard, with their palms cupped, so that it made a hollow sound, like wood knocked on wood. Then the men took it up. Then everybody. All round the fire, on the slow beat. Clap. Clap. Clap. And the quick drum rolling over it, and the deep drum thumping under it, and the sound going up into the starry dark over Last Thorn like smoke.
Lyra sat with her hot stone in her lap and did not know what to do with her hands.
Then Arran stood up.
He put the bone flute to his lips. And played. Not the three notes. Not the silly goat tune. A real tune. Quick and high and bright, that went up and down and round and in and out between the beats of the drums the way a swallow goes in and out between the trees. It was the happiest sound Lyra had heard since she could not remember when.
And the children got up and danced.
They did not dance the way people danced at the balls on the Hill, in pairs, in lines, in rows, with their hands held just so and their eyes on their partners' shoulders. They danced the way puppies run. All at once, in a crowd, round and round the fire in a ragged ring, stamping on the slow beat with their felt-wrapped feet, spinning, jumping, flinging their arms out, their round shaved heads bobbing and their painted lines shining in the firelight. Shrieking. Laughing. The girl who had thrown her spear was in the middle of them, spinning so fast her fur cape flew out round her like a bell.
Lyra watched them.
She was smiling. She could feel it on her face. She did not try to stop it.
And then a small hand took hold of hers.
She looked down. It was the little boy with the runny nose, from the path. He was standing in front of her, very serious, with his small cold hand round two of her fingers, pulling.
"No," said Lyra. "No, I can't. I don't know how."
He did not understand her. Or he did, and did not care. He pulled. Another child came, a girl, and took her other hand, and pulled too. And then there were three of them, four, pulling at her hands and her sleeves and the hem of her coat, laughing, and the hot stone slid out of her lap onto the mat, and she was on her feet.
"No," she said again, laughing. "No, really, I..."
And she was in the ring.
The drums were all round her. The quick one and the deep one. The clapping. The flute going in and out like a swallow. The children had her by both hands, and they were going round, round the fire, stamping, and she was going with them, stumbling in her clumsy felt-wrapped feet, the fire hot on one side of her face and the cold dark on the other.
She did not know the steps. There were no steps. The children just went round and stamped and spun and jumped, and she tried to do what they did, and could not, and tripped, and they laughed at her, and she laughed too.
And then the flute changed.
Arran had begun to play something slower. Not much. A little slower. And it had a shape to it, now. Three beats, and a little lift, and three beats again. One, two, three. One, two, three. And on the third, the flute went up, and hung, and came down.
And Lyra's feet knew it.
She did not tell them to. She did not think. Her feet heard the three beats and the lift, and something in them that had been asleep for a long time woke up, all at once, the way your hand wakes up when you have been lying on it.
One, two, three. Turn.
The hall at Crown Walk.
Not a picture. She did not see it. She did not need to. It was in her feet. The long hall downstairs with the black and white floor and the tall windows down one side, and the evening light coming in gold, and all the furniture pushed back against the walls. And her mother. Holding both her hands. Bending down, because Lyra was small, so small, five, six. And counting. One, two, three. And turn. One, two, three. And turn. Her mother's skirts brushing her face as they went round. Her mother's voice, laughing, counting. The black and white squares going by under her feet.
One, two, three. Turn.
Her feet did it. In the felt. On the frozen ground. By the fire. With the children's hands in hers.
One, two, three, and she lifted, a little, on her toes, on the third, the way her mother had taught her, so that she seemed to float. And turn. And she turned, under the children's arms, and her coat swung out round her, and the firelight spun.
The children stopped.
They stood still in the ring, holding her hands, and stared at her.
And she did it again. She could not stop. One, two, three, and lift, and turn. And again. Her feet knew every beat. The felt did not matter. The frozen ground did not matter. She was in the hall at Crown Walk with the gold light coming in, and her mother was counting, and she was six years old, and she was dancing.
And she laughed.
Out loud. Not the little surprised laugh that had come out of her by the bread stones, or the helpless one in the tent. Something else. Something she had not heard come out of her in so long that she did not know it. A long, high, clear laugh, with her head back, and her eyes shut, and the firelight on her face. A girl's laugh. A happy one. The laugh of somebody who has forgotten, for one whole moment, everything that has ever happened to her.
The children took it up. They began to copy her. One, two, three, and lift, and turn. Badly. Falling over. Laughing. And then Arran's flute went faster again, and the drums went faster, and the whole ring of them went round the fire, spinning and lifting and turning and falling over, with Lyra Thorne in the middle of them, dancing her mother's dance, and laughing, and laughing, and laughing.
She did not look for Corin. Not then. She did not look for anybody. For once in her life, she was not watching anyone at all.
What It Sounds Like
The flute stopped first. Then the drums, one after the other, the deep one and then the quick one, with a last little roll, like rain stopping. Then the clapping broke up into ordinary applause and shouting and laughter, and the ring of children fell apart, and three of them fell over on purpose in a heap, and the camp cheered.
Lyra stood by the fire with her chest heaving and her face burning and her hair stuck to her forehead with sweat, in the cold. Her felt-wrapped feet ached. Her arms, from the two hundred and one swings, ached worse. She did not care.
The little boy with the runny nose was still holding her hand. He looked up at her and said something in the round Ashborn speech, very seriously, and then let go and ran off to his mother.
"He says you dance like a heron," said Arran, coming past with his flute. He was grinning, the old wide grin, with all his teeth. "It's a compliment. Herons are the best dancers there are. They dance on one leg in the reeds in spring. We've all seen them."
Lyra laughed. She could not stop laughing tonight.
Then she turned round to go back to her mat, and her hot stone, and her place by the fire.
And saw Corin.
He had not moved. He was sitting exactly where he had been all evening, on the far side of the fire, with his crutch on the ground beside him and his bowl in his lap and his gray hands round it. But he was not eating. He was not listening to the stories. He was not doing anything at all.
He was looking at her.
Not the way he usually looked at her. Not the careful, puzzled, polite look, like a man reading a page he has been told is important and cannot quite understand. Something else. His face had gone very still. Completely still. The way a face goes when someone hears a sound in the night and is listening to find out what it was. His eyes were wide. His lips were a little apart.
She stopped.
The noise of the camp went on all round them. People laughing. Children shrieking. Someone starting up the quick drum again, softly, for no reason. But between her and Corin, across the low fire, there was a kind of quiet.
She went round the fire to him. Slowly. She did not know why she was going slowly.
"What?" she said, when she got there. "What is it? You look like you've seen a ghost."
He did not answer at once. He was still looking at her face.
Then he said, very quietly, not to her, not to anyone:
"That's it."
Lyra stood very still.
"That's it," said Corin again. "That's what it sounds like."
"What does?"
He looked up at her. And she saw that his eyes were wet.
"Your voice," he said. "When you're happy."
She could not move.
"I asked you," said Corin slowly. "At Thistle Ford. In the loft. It's in the book. I asked you what your voice sounds like when you're happy, and you said, you'll know it. And I didn't think I would. I didn't think I'd ever..." He stopped. "I've got your voice saying my name. That's all I've got. That's the only thing. Quick. A bit cross. Like you're telling me off. That's how I know you. That's all."
The fire crackled.
"And just now," said Corin, "you laughed. In the middle of all of them. With your head back. And I heard it." His voice was very low. "And I knew it. I knew it the way I know my name. Before I knew it was you. I heard it across the fire and I thought, that's her. That's her happy. That's what it sounds like."
Lyra did not say anything. She could not.
She stood there in front of him, with her face burning, and her breath going in and out, and all the noise of the camp round her, and looked down at him. At his gray hands round the bowl. At his wet eyes. And something happened in her chest that she did not have a name for. Something that hurt, and was not pain.
He had not remembered her. She knew that. He never would. He had told her so himself, in the dark, between the tents, last night. I don't know you. I don't have you.
But he had heard her laugh, and known it.
Not from the book. Not from anything she had told him. New. Tonight. For the first time.
And he had known it.
Corin had put down his bowl. He had his hand inside his coat. He was taking out the green book, and the pencil. And opening it, on his knee, by the firelight, and bending over it, close. Writing. At once. The way he did everything that mattered. Before it could get away.
She watched him do it. She did not look over his shoulder. For once, she did not read what he wrote.
She did not need to.
When he had finished, he shut the book and put it away inside his coat again, and pressed his hand flat on it, once. And looked up at her.
"There," he said. "Now I've got it twice. In me, and on paper. In case."
And Lyra, who had not cried at her father's deathbed and had cried on the gravel shelf at the edge of the thorns until she had nothing left, sat down on the mat beside him, all at once, and put her face in her hands, and did not know whether she was laughing or crying, and did not care.
Across the fire, Arran had picked up his flute again. He was not playing anything. He was only holding it, turning it in his long fingers, the way he did when he was bored.
The drums had stopped.
It was very late.
The Flute Stops
The camp did not sleep that night. Not properly. Not the way it had slept on the night of the rite, all together round the fire. People went to their tents, in ones and twos, with their children. But the fires outside the tents were kept up. And at the south edge of the camp, where the thorn slope came down from the Lip, there were sentries.
Lyra could see them from where she sat. Four of them, in a line, among the first of the thorn bushes. Dark shapes against the faint gray of the snow on the slope. Two men and two women, with bone spears, standing very still, facing south. Every so often one of them would move, stamp his feet against the cold, and then be still again.
And Arran was with them.
He had gone up there after the dancing. He did not say why. He only picked up his spear and his flute and a fur, and went, and Kestrel watched him go and did not stop him. Now he was sitting on a rock a little way up the slope from the other sentries, a dark thin shape with the fur round his shoulders, facing south, toward the Lip.
Playing.
Lyra could hear it from the fire. Very faint. Carried down the slope on the cold still air. The three notes. Low, high, a little lower. And a stop. Over and over. Lazily. The way a man drums his fingers on a table while he waits.
What you play when you're bored.
She sat by the fire with her hot stone in her lap and her arms aching and listened to it.
Corin was asleep. He had fallen asleep sitting up, beside her, with his head against her shoulder. She had not moved him. She did not want to. His breath was slow and even. Every now and then, in his sleep, the hum came, very faint, and went again.
Oren was not asleep. He was sitting on her other side with his sword across his knees and his whetstone in his hand, drawing it along the blade, slowly, with his eyes half shut. The soft steady scrape of it went on and on.
Vespera was asleep on a mat by the fire, curled up very small under a fur, with her rope belt of needles laid out beside her where she could reach it.
Kestrel was not asleep either. She was sitting on the bare earth on the north side of the fire, facing the ridge and the Glass, the way she always sat, with her long arms round her knees. But her head was turned. Over her shoulder. South. Toward the sentries. Toward Arran's flute.
The three notes. And the stop. And the three notes.
The fire burned down. Oren put more thorn on it. The flames came up yellow and then sank to red.
Lyra's eyes began to close. She let them. She thought, just for a moment. Just for a little while. Corin's head was warm on her shoulder and the hot stone was warm in her lap and the scrape of Oren's whetstone was steady and the three notes went round and round on the slope above, low, high, a little lower, and stop.
Low. High.
And stopped.
In the middle.
Lyra's eyes opened.
She did not know why. Nothing had happened. There had been no sound. No shout. Nothing.
That was it. Nothing. The flute had stopped. Not at the end of the three notes, where it always stopped, where it paused and started again. In the middle. On the second note. As if Arran had taken it away from his mouth all at once.
She lifted her head.
Beside her, the scrape of Oren's whetstone had stopped too.
Across the fire, Kestrel was on her feet. Lyra had not seen her get up. She was standing, very tall and very still, with her face turned south, toward the slope.
The camp was silent.
Not the quiet of a camp asleep. Another kind. The kind of silence that comes when a great many people hold their breath at once.
And then Lyra heard it.
Faint. Far off. Up the slope, in the dark, beyond the sentries and the rock where Arran sat. A sound she had never heard before in her life, and knew at once, the way you know thunder.
Ticking.
Steady. Patient. Many of them, all together. Not quite in time with each other, and then, as she listened, falling into time. Tick. Tick. Tick. Like a roomful of clocks.
Like the clockmaker's shop on Vellum Row, Lyra thought, that she had passed as a little girl with her hand in her father's, where a hundred clocks ticked on the walls behind the glass and she had stood with her nose against the window and listened. Like that. But not behind glass. Coming down a hill. Through the thorns. In the dark.
Closer.
Corin's head came up off her shoulder. All at once. Awake. She felt him go rigid beside her. Felt him listen.
The hum in his throat had stopped.
"That's them," he said, very low.
Oren was on his feet. The sword was in his hand. The whetstone had gone into his pocket. He did not say anything. He did not need to.
On the slope above, a dark thin shape stood up off a rock. Arran. He had the flute in one hand and the spear in the other. He was looking up the slope, into the dark, toward the sound.
And then he turned, and ran. Down the slope. Toward the camp. Toward the fire. Not shouting. Not calling out. Running, in his felt-wrapped feet, as fast as Lyra had ever seen anyone run, with the fur flying off his shoulders and falling behind him in the snow.
The ticking came on behind him.
Tick. Tick. Tick.
And it was not tomorrow. It was not the day after. It was not two fingers.
It was now.
